hook: Sloths lose thirty percent of body weight in one bathroom trip

scenes.line: A sloth spends most of its life hanging motionless in rainforest canopies.
scenes.visual_prompt: A three-toed sloth clinging to a thick tree branch, surrounded by dense green leaves and vines, dappled sunlight filtering through the canopy, absolutely still and serene.

scenes.line: They move so slowly that algae grows on their fur, turning them green.
scenes.visual_prompt: Close-up of sloth fur with moss and algae visibly coating the hair strands, creating a greenish-brown camouflage pattern blending into tree bark and lichen.

scenes.line: But here's the weird part: they only poop once every seven days.
scenes.visual_prompt: A calendar page showing seven days passing, with a glowing red circle around day seven, surrounded by question marks and symbols of biological urgency.

scenes.line: When they finally go, they literally shed up to a third of their weight.
scenes.visual_prompt: An illustrated silhouette of a sloth split in two—one side full and heavy, the other noticeably smaller and lighter, with a downward arrow between them showing the dramatic reduction.

scenes.line: This weekly toilet trip forces them down to the forest floor, exposing them.
scenes.visual_prompt: A sloth descending a massive tree trunk toward shadowy undergrowth below, surrounded by looming predator silhouettes—jaguars and snakes—waiting in the leafy darkness.

scenes.line: Poachers and predators now hunt sloths specifically during these vulnerable moments.
scenes.visual_prompt: Dark silhouettes of armed figures moving through misty rainforest undergrowth, with camera traps and nets visible among tangled roots and fallen leaves.

scenes.line: Their bizarre digestive system—designed for a leafy diet—is now their downfall.
scenes.visual_prompt: An anatomical cross-section diagram showing a sloth's enlarged stomach and slow digestive tract, with clock symbols indicating the week-long processing time, fading into a fading rainforest landscape.

cta: Would you risk weekly exposure to predators for that kind of digestive efficiency, or is weekly bathroom trips worth the danger?
